short: Ballistarii (Latin) - soldiers assigned as personnel to throwing machines, including ballistae. In case of their unavailability, the manuballista (hand ballista) became their primary weapon. One of the reliefs of the Arch of Constantine depicts two infantry soldiers wearing strange cylindrical-shaped headgear, which are fixed with straps passed under the chin of the soldiers. The headgear, which are obviously a variant of Pannonian hats, are covered by small bolts, no more than 20 cm long, having plumage on one end and a ball-shaped thickening in the middle. These bolts are held in place by a strap spanning the soldier's cap. It is assumed that this bas-relief depicts ballistari armed with manuballistae. According to F. Richardo, the widespread use of manuballistae at the end of the 4th century indicates that the protective armament had significantly improved for the barbarians who attacked the Empire along the Rhine-Danube border. Despite its compact size, the manuballista was a powerful weapon. According to experiments conducted in 1979, the manuballista could throw arrows to a range of 285 metres.
history: In the face of an increasing number of barbarian incursions, the effective defence of Rome’s now-sprawling territory became a serious problem in the 4th century AD. The Emperor Constantine’s controversial solution was to divide the army into two halves. 'Limitanei', literally ‘the men on the limes’ or 'borders', were frontier garrison troops intended to pin down an invading force until the full-time 'comitatenses', the late-Roman equivalent of the traditional Legionaries, could arrive to deal with the situation decisively. Although well-equipped, limitanei were generally considered by all to be second-class warriors. This was possibly because they were often part-time soldiers who had been encouraged to settle and farm the land around their outposts in exchange for policing the Empire's borders.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
